clips.text_zh: 成班人傾緊 Cybercab 買返嚟再放上 Tesla Robotaxi network 收租。靠車揾 passive income 真係 work 嗎？當 robotaxi 真係 fully autonomous，我哋呢啲 surveying 廢柴係咪都可以被動收入？btw Elon 講過 Optimus 同 FSD 嘅 progress，係咪應該 long TSLA？🧐
clips.text_en_b1: Redpill me on buying Cybercabs and putting them to work on the Tesla Robotaxi network for passive income. If Tesla really gets to unsupervised Full Self-Driving, can a regular person buy a fleet of Cybercabs and earn money while sleeping? What are the real numbers on utilization, depreciation, and Musk's timeline for actually launching the robotaxi service?
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread on Cybercab + Tesla Robotaxi passive income

signal.rationale: OP is implicitly bullish on Tesla's robotaxi fleet economics, which is a long TSLA thesis

clips.text_en_b2: Talk me into buying a fleet of Cybercabs and putting them to work on Tesla's Robotaxi network for some genuine passive income. Assuming Tesla actually pulls off unsupervised Full Self-Driving, could an ordinary person realistically run a small fleet and earn money round the clock? I want to see the hard numbers on utilisation rates, depreciation curves, and whether Musk's robotaxi rollout timeline is anything more than another promise that slips by two years.
clips.text_en_c1: I'm trying to get a sober assessment of the Cybercab-as-passive-income thesis that has been making the rounds across /biz/. Assuming Tesla ultimately cracks unsupervised Full Self-Driving, what would the realistic unit economics actually look like for a retail investor running, say, a five-vehicle fleet on the Robotaxi network? Specifically, I'd like to see hard figures on daily utilization rates, residual depreciation curves over a seven-year horizon, insurance premia, and whether Musk's stated launch timeline—which has slipped repeatedly—can be trusted at face value. Anecdotally the bull case hinges on Optimus synergies and FSD generalization, but I've been burned by similar narratives before.
clips.text_en_c2: I'm looking for a sober assessment of the thesis that one ought to accumulate Cybercabs and deploy them onto Tesla's nascent Robotaxi network as a passive-income instrument. Assuming the company eventually arrives at genuinely unsupervised Full Self-Driving, what would the unit economics actually look like for an individual owner-operator running a small fleet? I'm particularly curious about realistic utilization rates, depreciation curves across a typical vehicle lifespan, and whether Musk's publicly stated timeline for the commercial launch warrants any credence. Separately, given the recent Optimus demonstrations and incremental FSD refinements, would you be inclined to underwrite a long TSLA position on the assumption that these programmes converge into a coherent autonomous-services platform, or is the valuation already pricing in far more than the underlying engineering can deliver?

clips.text_zh: 又睇到 biz 有人問：如果只可以 hold 一個 10 年，你揀 Bitcoin 定 gold？我啲 prop firm account 又輸緊，CFD 都係 red。黃金同 BTC 都係我嘅 hedge，但 10 年 scale 我真係唔識揀。🙏 命理都冇講呢樣。
clips.text_en_b1: Bitcoin vs Gold. If you had to hold only one for the next 10 years, would you choose Bitcoin or gold? What makes your choice better than the other? I'm trying to decide where to put the small amount of capital I have left after blowing up my prop firm and CFD accounts this year.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread on 10-year BTC vs gold thesis

signal.rationale: OP is framing a 10-year holding decision between BTC and gold with no clear entry or exit levels

clips.text_en_b2: Bitcoin or gold — if you could only hold one asset for the next ten years, which would you pick and why is it clearly superior? I've blown up my prop firm and CFD accounts earlier this year, so I'm working with whatever capital I have left and trying to park it somewhere sensible. Both have served as hedges, but on a decade-long timescale I genuinely cannot decide where my money belongs.
clips.text_en_c1: I've been wrestling with an allocation question that has resurfaced on /biz/ and I'd appreciate a rigorous answer. Suppose you were forced to hold a single asset for the next decade, no rebalancing, no leverage, no exit—you had to choose between Bitcoin and physical gold. Which would you pick, and what is the underlying thesis that distinguishes your conviction from the other camp? Both function as macro hedges in my book, but on a ten-year risk-adjusted basis I genuinely cannot determine which dominates.
clips.text_en_c2: Settle a protracted internal debate, if you would. Constrained to a single asset held for the next decade, would your conviction lie with Bitcoin or with physical gold, and what precisely underwrites that conviction beyond reflexive tribal allegiance? I've haemorrhaged capital this year through an ill-advised prop firm account and a spectacularly mistimed CFD position, leaving me with a modest residual sum that I am exceedingly reluctant to squander. Both instruments ostensibly function as hedges against monetary debasement, yet their ten-year trajectories diverge markedly in volatility profile, regulatory exposure, and correlation to risk assets. Which, in your considered judgement, offers the superior asymmetry once you account for tail risk, custody friction, and the non-trivial probability that one of them simply ceases to matter?

clips.text_zh: CloseAI 出咗個新 Astra model，自稱 AGI。/g/ 班友已經開串。工程仔都知 survey 行最先俾 AI 搞掂，白領就嚟緊。HKIE 考牌都未搞掂，AI 已經黎緊搶我哋飯碗。wtf 🧐
clips.text_en_b1: CloseAI new Astra model. They claim it is AGI. So… what's your verdict, /g/? Is this actually AGI or just another marketing wrapper around a bigger LLM? I work in surveying and engineering, and I'm honestly worried the blue-collar jobs are going first, then white-collar follows.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread on CloseAI's claimed AGI model 'Astra'

signal.rationale: Tech/AI discussion, not a trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: CloseAI just dropped their new Astra model and they're claiming it amounts to AGI, so /g/, what's your honest verdict? Is this genuinely a leap forward or simply a slick marketing exercise wrapped around yet another inflated LLM? Working in surveying has made me uneasy, because the entry-level engineering roles are clearly being automated first, and if that's any indication, white-collar work won't be far behind.
clips.text_en_c1: CloseAI has unveiled its latest model, codenamed Astra, and the marketing materials are once again claiming we have arrived at AGI. Given how liberally that term has been thrown around over the past eighteen months, I'm inclined to treat the announcement with considerable skepticism—but I'd like to hear /g/'s technical verdict rather than relying on hype cycles. Is there genuinely something architecturally novel here, or is Astra essentially a repackaged wrapper around the same underlying scaling playbook dressed up with new branding? As someone working in surveying and engineering, I find the labour-displacement implications rather uncomfortable: surveying appears to be among the earliest white-collar professions to face genuine automation risk,…
clips.text_en_c2: CloseAI's freshly unveiled Astra model purportedly constitutes AGI, and the engineering contingent on /g/ is, predictably, already lacerating the claim with considerable relish. Setting aside the marketing apparatus, what is your genuine adjudication: does this represent a genuine inflection in capability, or is it yet another veneer draped over an incrementally larger language model with a more compelling demo reel? As someone employed in the surveying profession, I find the discourse disquieting; the consensus seems to be that surveying and adjacent engineering disciplines will be the first white-collar professions absorbed, while the blue-collar tranche was always the easier target. Should I be quietly updating my CV whilst quietly despairing at the prospect of professional obsolescence arriving before my HKIE qualification does?

clips.text_zh: 中國互聯網又出咗新潮流，叫「bubble chin」。一堆女 influencer 帶頭做。HK 啲女仔遲早跟，我返茶記食飯睇到都唔知笑定喊。lol 呢啲嘢同我考 HKIE 完全冇關，但又食花生。
clips.text_en_b1: Newest trend in China just dropped. Chinese internet users are calling it the bubble chin. It's becoming increasingly fashionable among Chinese female influencers on Weibo and Xiaohongshu, with cosmetic clinics reporting a surge in hyaluronic acid filler bookings for the chin area this quarter.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread on Chinese 'bubble chin' influencer trend

signal.rationale: HK/news cultural observation, no trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: Looks like Chinese internet has rolled out yet another cosmetic trend, this one dubbed the bubble chin. A slew of female influencers across Weibo and Xiaohongshu are showcasing the look, and apparently cosmetic clinics have seen bookings for hyaluronic acid fillers in the chin area surge this quarter. Cosmetic fashion fads come and go, but this particular one has caught on alarmingly fast across multiple platforms simultaneously.
clips.text_en_c1: A curious aesthetic has begun propagating across Chinese social media platforms, one that locals have dubbed the "bubble chin" trend. It appears to have originated among mid-tier female influencers on Weibo and Xiaohongshu, who have been showcasing exaggerated, rounded chin profiles achieved through targeted hyaluronic acid filler injections. Cosmetic clinics in tier-one cities are reportedly seeing booking volumes surge this quarter, which suggests the trend has crossed from niche internet curiosity into something resembling a genuine consumer movement. Whether this bleeds into Hong Kong's beauty circles within the next six months is anyone's guess, but the pattern of Mainland trends migrating south has held remarkably consistent in recent years.
clips.text_en_c2: The Chinese internet, in its infinite capacity to generate aesthetic peculiarity, has apparently bestowed upon us the 'bubble chin,' a cosmetic augmentation propagated with customary zeal by a cohort of Weibo and Xiaohongshu influencers who evidently view their mandibles as insufficiently prominent. Cosmetic clinics across tier-one cities are reporting a precipitous surge in hyaluronic acid filler bookings for the chin region this quarter, which says rather more about the prevailing beauty standards than any honest anatomical assessment warrants. Hong Kong will, with the predictability of monsoon season, follow suit within months. I observe this phenomenon from a cha chaan teng with an ambivalence that defies tidy categorisation: simultaneously amused, mildly appalled, and grateful that my own HKIE examinations occupy my attention sufficiently to preclude extended contemplation of anyone's chin-related life choices.

clips.text_zh: 打機打到悶，去 /v/ 睇到有人問 Fallout 4 真係有冇傳說中咁好。我就 S15 排位打到喊，練下英文睇下遊戲 review 當 chill。考牌溫書溫到傻，轉吓 channel。lol
clips.text_en_b1: Is Fallout 4 really as good as people say it is? When I first played it, it felt like a game that was developed too quickly and rushed to release. The gunplay felt stiff, the dialogue system was a downgrade from New Vegas, and the main story ended in a way that ignored half your companions. Why do people still call it a masterpiece?
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread debating Fallout 4 quality vs nostalgia

signal.rationale: Gaming/culture discussion, not a trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: Is Fallout 4 genuinely worth the legendary reputation it still carries, or has nostalgia done the heavy lifting? Having finally given it a proper go, I came away convinced the game was rushed out the door — the gunplay feels clunky compared to modern shooters, the dialogue system is a clear downgrade from New Vegas, and the ending somehow manages to sideline half the companions you spent hours levelling up.
clips.text_en_c1: After growing thoroughly bored with ranked grinding, I wandered into a /v/ thread debating whether Fallout 4 genuinely deserves the reputation it commands, and I found myself unexpectedly sympathetic to the contrarian position. On my first playthrough years ago, the game struck me as having been pushed through certification under considerable time pressure—the gunplay felt weighty in a way that bordered on clunky, the dialogue system represented a clear regression from New Vegas's branching complexity, and the main narrative resolved in a manner that effectively sidelined roughly half the companion roster. The open-world moment-to-moment gameplay remained compelling, yet structural criticisms seemed valid.
clips.text_en_c2: Burnt out from grinding ranked matches to no avail, I wandered into a /v/ thread posing the heretical question of whether Fallout 4 genuinely merits its canonical status or whether collective nostalgia has done the heavy lifting for Bethesda's marketing department. When I first installed it, the gunplay struck me as curiously wooden for a 2015 title, the dialogue wheel represented a regressive step from New Vegas's branching architecture, and the main quest concluded in a manner that rather pointedly ignored half the companions I'd invested in emotionally. So I pose the question to the thread at large: is the lingering reverence a function of genuine design merit, or merely the inertia of a franchise whose acronym alone guarantees purchase? Reluctant to surrender my evenings entirely to exam revision, I defer to the assembled connoisseurs.

clips.text_zh: 肥仔信今日又 push 我去打 BJJ。/fit/ 啲佬講得好啱：你 bench 315 都唔代表你打得贏輕你 50 磅嘅 grappler。我哋 MMA circle 真係要返去練地板戰，唔做細佬。🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Hey nice bench press anon, 315 lbs really impressive! Anyhow, any grappler would have you staring at your own asshole in seconds. You have no reason to not train grappling, unless you want some guy who weighs 50 pounds less than you to make you his bitch. Even if you deadlift him off the ground, half-decent BJJ controls you instantly.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread arguing lifting bros must also train grappling
clips.text_en_b2: Nice bench press numbers, 315 pounds is genuinely impressive, though any halfway decent grappler would have you folded like a lawn chair within seconds regardless. There's simply no excuse for skipping grappling entirely, unless you're perfectly content letting some dude half your size turn you into his personal training dummy. Even if you somehow deadlift him clean off the ground, half-competent BJJ will have him controlling you before your feet even touch the mat.
clips.text_en_c1: Credit where it's due—anonymous benching 315 pounds represents genuinely impressive upper-body strength, and nobody in their right mind would dismiss that achievement outright. The uncomfortable truth that /fit/ routinely reminds us of, however, is that raw pressing power translates poorly into a live grappling exchange; any competent BJJ practitioner of comparable size could likely have that same lifter tapping within seconds, regardless of how much weight he moves on the barbell. The disparity becomes even more pronounced when you consider an opponent who weighs fifty pounds lighter yet possesses solid fundamentals—superior leverage, hip positioning, and submission entries would render deadlift strength largely irrelevant.
clips.text_en_c2: Commendations upon the commendable bench press, anon; a 315 lift is no mean physiological feat, and you should derive legitimate satisfaction therefrom. Be that as it may, any competent grappler of merely adequate training would consign you to studying the ceiling in a matter of seconds, assuming you ever managed to close the distance before being folded like laundry. There exists no intellectually defensible reason to forgo grappling instruction unless your preference is to be thoroughly dominated by a man half a hundred pounds your junior, who could no doubt be deadlifted clean off the mat and yet would have you utterly neutralised within a single exchange.

clips.text_zh: 夜晚溫書溫到悶，上 /a/ 吹水。見到條 post 問：如果你係真 anime fan，即刻講一個 Fairy Tail 角色名出嚟，唔可以係 Lucy。我答 Erza，OK？btw Gundam 00 雙人駕駛先係神作。👍
clips.text_en_b1: If you're a true anime fan, mention (1) Fairy Tail character off the bat that is not Lucy. Not Natsu either, because that's the obvious answer. I'm doing a personality quiz on /a/ tonight and so far the only answers that count are Erza Scarlet, Gray Fullbuster, and Juvia Lockser, since most casual viewers can't name a third character from the guild.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread on 'real anime fan' Fairy Tail quiz
clips.text_en_b2: Stumbled across a thread on /a/ tonight running a quick personality quiz for self-proclaimed anime fans, and the first question asks you to name a Fairy Tail character off the top of your head that isn't Lucy or Natsu. Apparently the only answers they count as legitimate are Erza Scarlet, Gray Fullbuster, and Juvia Lockser, because the casual viewers overwhelmingly fail to name a third guild member beyond the obvious ones.
clips.text_en_c1: I stumbled across an /a/ thread this evening purporting to separate the genuine anime enthusiasts from the casual viewers, and the diagnostic question struck me as rather clever. The prompt asks participants to name a Fairy Tail character within thirty seconds, with Lucy and Natsu explicitly disqualified as obvious choices—ostensibly because the test is designed to filter out viewers whose familiarity with the series extends only as far as its two most marketable protagonists. The only answers that apparently register as legitimate are Erza Scarlet, Gray Fullbuster, and Juvia Lockser, which suggests the bar for passage is admittedly modest.
clips.text_en_c2: Beleaguered by revision and seeking succour in the ambient chaos of /a/, I encountered a thread that posed what purported to be the definitive litmus test of authentic anime literacy: name, without perceptible hesitation, a Fairy Tail character who is neither Lucy nor Natsu, the latter being altogether too facile an answer. I proffered Erza Scarlet and now await the tribunal's verdict, though I suspect Gray Fullbuster or Juvia Lockser would have demonstrated marginally more discriminating taste, given that the casual viewership terminates abruptly at protagonist-tier recognition. The exercise, whilst admittedly contrived, does illuminate a starker truth: most self-professed devotees retain roughly two-and-a-half character names per guild before their fluency collapses entirely.
